The Australia Institute proposed a wealth tax on assets over $5 million. Noel Whittaker argues this will drive investment away and hurt productivity.

The Poison:
The article relies on speculative fear of capital flight rather than empirical data on the tax's actual economic impact.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
The article confuses the *proposal* (a policy tool) with the *outcome* (economic collapse), a classic Reductive Plane Error.

Social Physics Analysis:
The article runs a Smart Selfish Maneuver: it frames a tax on the ultra-wealthy as a threat to everyone's productivity, using fear to protect existing capital structures.

The Trajectory: The Path of Fall into Destruction.
Modal Dynamics: can be -> is not via Reductive Geodesic. The article takes a potential policy solution and declares it a systemic impossibility.

The Unavoidable Truth: Wealth taxes are a legitimate policy tool for addressing inequality.
The Unavoidable Lie: Any tax on wealth will inevitably destroy the entire economy.

The article prioritizes the protection of existing capital over the systemic need for revenue, framing a policy debate as an existential threat.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Just how many times do governments expect to tax the same investment?

Australia doesn't have a wealth problem, but a productivity problem.

Actual Article Body:

Just when we thought we had enough to worry about, along comes another bright idea: an annual wealth tax on Australians who have had the temerity to accumulate a few million dollars.

Login or signup to continue reading

The proposal comes from the Australia Institute, which reckons a 2 per cent annual tax on net wealth above $5 million, excluding the family home and superannuation, would raise $41 billion a year. Add the abolition of the 50 per cent capital gains tax discount and the return of inheritance taxes, and the institute estimates an extra $70 billion annually. It sounds like the answer to every treasurer's prayers.

Wealth and income are two entirely different things. Somebody may own a valuable business, farm or investment properties without having the cash to pay an annual tax on their value. Imagine a farmer with $10 million worth of land, struggling to make a profit but facing a hefty tax bill because the land has increased in value on paper. And who decides what everything is worth? Listed shares are straightforward, but private companies, farms and family trusts are another matter. Annual valuations would mean enormous costs, disputes and court cases. Accountants and lawyers might be delighted, but how would any of this improve productivity?

Before Australian politicians get too enthusiastic, they should look at California, where a one-off 5 five per cent tax on billionaires has been proposed to raise tens of billions, principally for healthcare. Supporters argue that people with enormous fortunes can afford to contribute more. It's an attractive proposition, particularly to voters who won't pay it themselves. But wealthy people can change where they live and invest, and governments cannot assume they'll behave as revenue forecasts predict.

Some of California's richest residents have reportedly reconsidered their arrangements. Economists warn that if billionaires relocate, the state could lose substantial ongoing income tax revenue. The damage could extend well beyond those individuals. Entrepreneurs establish businesses, employ people, attract investment and generate taxes year after year. If their next venture goes elsewhere, the consequences may outlast any one-off...
